description: We're a team of three—Shaheen Amir, Amisha Sharma, and Deep Desai—passionate about technology, innovation, and space exploration. Our interests include AI, software engineering, data analysis, and creative problem-solving. We're excited to tackle the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge by developing an interactive, data-driven solution using NASA resources. We look forward to combining our skills to build an innovative and meaningful solution!
summary:
We built LunaNav, a web app that helps early-stage lunar mission planners pick the south-pole landing site and dates where a lander can talk to Earth.

At the south pole, Earth sits on the horizon and rocks with libration, so ridges and crater rims keep blocking the direct line of sight to Earth. Relay satellites can fill the gaps, but measuring how much they help at one site on one date today takes JPL Horizons, NASA terrain data, relay orbits and a specialist with their own pipeline.

LunaNav does it in one workflow. Pick a site, a mission window and a relay setup. Every 10 minutes, LunaNav checks whether Earth is above the real terrain skyline, whether a complete lander → relay → Earth path exists, and whether the Sun is up. It then reports coverage, every blackout and the longest blackout, direct versus relay-assisted, side by side. It answers the challenge's question (where are the Sun and Earth relative to the local horizon?) and the planning question that follows from it.

Why it matters: over 1 Jan–1 Apr 2027, direct-to-Earth line of sight covers only 47% of the time at Connecting Ridge and 45% at Shackleton Rim, with gaps of almost two weeks. With NASA's LCRNS reference relays (simulated), both reach 100% geometric line of sight. Planners can see that before they commit to a site.
details:
What exactly does it do?

1. Pick a south-pole landing site: Connecting Ridge or Shackleton Rim (NASA 5 m terrain), or 9 more precomputed sites (120 m terrain).

2. Pick a mission start date and duration inside the supported window (1 Jan–1 Apr 2027).

3. See direct-to-Earth line of sight against the real terrain horizon, plus Sun and Earth elevation, every 10 minutes (12,961 samples per site).

4. Turn on a simulated relay setup: NASA's LCRNS reference constellation (5 satellites in elliptical frozen orbits, semi-major axis 11,316 km, eccentricity 0.692, apoapsis over the south pole), a single LCRNS satellite, or Lunar Pathfinder.

5. Read the coverage %, the list of blackouts and the longest blackout, direct versus relay-assisted.

6. Compare two sites, two dates or two relay setups side by side, and replay the mission in 3D from the lander's view of the sky.

How does it work?

- Sun and Earth: JPL Horizons gives the azimuth and elevation of the Sun and Earth seen from each site.

- Terrain skyline: from a 2 m antenna, we cast 720 rays, one every 0.5°, over NASA LOLA elevation data. We use 5 m PGDA models near the site and LDEM 120 m data out to 300 km, accounting for the Moon's curvature. The result is a 360° horizon.

- Relays: orbits are propagated from published orbital elements (two-body).

- Path rule: a sample counts as connected only when a complete path exists: Earth above the skyline, or a relay above the skyline that also sees Earth. A relay the lander sees but that can't see Earth doesn't count.

- Architecture: an offline Python pipeline writes compact JSON. A static Next.js app on Cloudflare Pages does all the analysis in the browser, so results update instantly. An optional "pick a point" server computes any south-pole point live with the same pipeline.

- Validation: across 18.6 years, our horizons for the 9 extra sites agree with NASA Moon Trek's Earth-visibility map within 7.4 percentage points. We also checked our path rule against NASA's LunaNet Interoperability Specification (LNIS v5).

What benefits does it have?

- An answer in seconds instead of a custom analysis: how often can this site see Earth on these dates, and how long is the worst blackout?

- It shows how much a relay network helps before the relays fly.

- It shows when power and a link line up. With LCRNS relays, the Sun is up and a link exists 94% of the time at Shackleton Rim and 49% at Connecting Ridge.

- It is honest about its limits. Every number traces to NASA data, and every metric is labeled "geometric line of sight".

What do you hope to achieve?

We want a fast first-look tool for Artemis-era south-pole missions. A planner should be able to compare sites, launch dates and relay options in minutes, and bring a sharper question to specialist link analysis. Next steps: add link budgets and DSN scheduling, model more relay networks as they are announced (ESA Moonlight), and extend coverage to more sites and longer windows.

Limitations

- Geometric line of sight only: no link budget, antennas, data rates, interference or DSN scheduling.

- Relays are simulated reference designs, not deployed satellites. LCRNS v3.1 is a government reference design. We model only relays from Artemis Accords signatories.

- Two-body orbits are good for coverage statistics, not for operations.

- Shackleton Rim sits on a crest: its direct-to-Earth figure ranges from 27% to 45% within 150 m, so treat it as a range.

Tools, languages, software

Python 3.12 (uv, NumPy, SciPy, rasterio) · JPL Horizons API · TypeScript · Next.js · React · Tailwind CSS · shadcn/ui · three.js (react-three-fiber, drei) · bun · Cloudflare Pages · GitHub · Tailscale Funnel (optional point server).
